best_guess.city: Costa Calma / Playitas–Las Playitas area, Fuerteventura

coarse_filters.approx_climate_biome: Hot arid / desert coastal (BWh), volcanic island, near-zero natural vegetation apart from planted Canary palms

cues.observation: Circular red-rimmed white speed-limit signs reading 90 on a dual carriageway — EU/Spanish convention; Spain's 90 km/h general limit on conventional/divided roads outside motorway status.
Traffic keeps right; New Jersey concrete median barrier with narrow planted strip, and slim tapered concrete-topped edge barriers typical of Spanish autovía/carretera construction on the Canaries.
Dark reddish-brown scoria/basalt hillside with almost no vegetation, thin ochre lapilli soil — young volcanic terrain, not sedimentary Mediterranean limestone.
Long rows of planted Phoenix canariensis (Canary Island date palm) along the highway, with only tussock/desert scrub as natural cover.
Yellow-and-white Mercedes Sprinter ambulance with orange striping, common Canarian SUC/private ambulance livery; European compact cars with white front / yellow rear plate proportions.

Large all-inclusive resort complex: whitewashed cubic blocks with orange-red pantile hipped roofs, low-rise sprawl, huge surface car park — the standard Fuerteventura/Lanzarote package-holiday resort typology.
Low rounded ochre hills without deep ravines, blue open ocean and a faint island/mountain silhouette on the horizon across a strait.
Terraced white apartment bungalow village stepping down a bare slope with tennis courts and walled compounds — a purpose-built tourist urbanización rather than an organic town.
Palm-lined quiet residential street, kerbside parking, older asphalt, faded white markings; hillside cut in loose volcanic rubble immediately adjacent — small-scale resort street grid.
Bright dry haze, dust-brown ground, no seasonal grass — extremely arid island, drier than Tenerife/Gran Canaria north sides.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A monoculture tourism economy: motorway-grade access road serving nothing but coastal resort clusters, rental-fleet cars (many identical small hatchbacks and a motorhome), all-inclusive hotel with private security walls and a large free car park. Land outside the resort walls is untouched desert with no farming — water and food are imported. Spanish/EU regulatory landscape (signage, ambulance service, road standards) combined with northern-European package-holiday clientele. Low local population density, high seasonal service employment, peripheral EU outermost-region character.

narrowing.discriminator: Lanzarote enforces a strict island-wide aesthetic code: white cubic buildings with GREEN (coast) or brown (interior) woodwork and flat roofs, and low-rise resorts almost never use large orange pantile hipped roofs or big pagoda-like roof masses. Fuerteventura's resorts freely use terracotta pantile hipped roofs over white walls, exactly as seen at the hotel here. The tall lone ridge of dark scoria beside a modern 2x2 coastal corridor also matches Fuerteventura's FV-2 / Jandía–Costa Calma stretch rather than Lanzarote's LZ roads.

ruled_out: Lanzarote — César Manrique building code (flat white roofs, green/brown woodwork) contradicts the orange pantile roofscape

narrowing.conclusion: Southern/eastern resort corridor of Fuerteventura — most likely the Costa Calma–Jandía or Playitas stretch where the divided highway hugs a scoria ridge above a walled resort

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A mono-functional international beach-resort economy: large all-inclusive hotel complexes (Fuerteventura Princess, Royal Palm), rental-fleet compact cars and a camper van, a Mercadona serving resort staff and self-catering tourists, plus a golf course inland. Wealth is imported (Northern European package tourism); the surrounding land is unfarmable volcanic desert, so almost all built form is post-1980 tourist development strung along the FV-2 highway. Spanish-language, Canarian regional culture with heavy German/British visitor presence.

narrative.blind_logic: The blind chain relies purely on visual cues: right-hand traffic, EU signage, and volcanic scoria terrain to reach Canary Islands, then uses roof architecture (orange pantile vs Lanzarote's mandated flat white/green code) to eliminate Lanzarote in favor of Fuerteventura, and finally uses road geometry (ridge-hugging dual carriageway, walled resort village, distant island silhouette) to guess at a southern resort corridor, landing tentatively on Costa Calma/Jandía/Playitas with 0.55 confidence, explicitly hedging between several candidate locations.
narrative.aided_logic: The aided chain follows a similar early trajectory (EU standards, Spain, Canary Islands, Fuerteventura via road-code prefix and terrain) but then pivots at admin_region and beyond to directly reading map-only data: the FV-2 road code, named landmarks (Monte Aguda 305m, Barranco de Vinamar, Boca de Esquinzo), and labeled POIs (Fuerteventura Princess, Royal Palm Resort, Jandía Golf, Morro Jable) that pin the location precisely to Esquinzo–Butihondo. The final district-level step even reasons about which side of the FV-2 the camera sits on relative to the map pin, reaching 0.9 confidence.
narrative.delta: The first three steps (continent, country, macro_region/country) are essentially unchanged in reasoning quality, both using genuine street-level visual evidence. The divergence begins at admin_region, where the aided chain adds the 'FV-2' road-code sign as a shortcut confirmation, but the decisive break is at metro_area and district: the blind chain builds a plausible but hedged guess from topography and architecture alone (ridge-hugging highway, walled resort, orange pantile roofs), while the aided chain simply reads off named map labels (Monte Aguda, Barranco de Vinamar, Fuerteventura Princess, Royal Palm Resort, Morro Jable) to assert an exact location. These labels could not be derived from the images and function as answer leakage rather than independent discrimination — the 'disc' text even cites the map pin's position directly ('the pin sits directly on the FV-2') as the discriminator.
